amendments.rule:
A verbless clause supplies its English copula from the construction, not from nothing. In *that it was good*, the supplied *it was* belongs to the unit headed on `טוֹב`; do not mark it `added`. **Where the ASV renders a verbless clause with a presentative *there was* or *there were*, the dummy *there* is part of the same construction-supplied frame as the copula and joins the unit that bears that copula under this rule, whether a nominal anchor or a prepositional predicate.** It is never `added`, and the unit still heads on its lexical predicate or anchor. **Apart from that presentative dummy, this covers the copula and nothing more.** Where the ASV instead supplies a whole *lexical* verb for a clause whose Hebrew has none — the allotment formula `וְלִבְנֵי קְהָת הַנּוֹתָרִים ... עָרִים עָשֶׂר` → *And unto the rest of the sons of Kohath* ***were given*** *by lot ... ten cities* — no morpheme's rendering that verb completes, and it is `added` under rule 30, together with any object the ASV supplies alongside it, as in *were given them*. Test by asking which morpheme is there to carry the English: `הָיָה` carries the *have* of rule 43 and the frame of rule 21, a Hebrew verb carries the light verb of rule 44, and a preposition that is itself the predicate carries the copula of rule 49 — but a preposition the ASV has already spent a word on, as in *unto the rest*, carries nothing further, and a clause with no verb in it at all licenses no verb. **The same lexical-verb boundary holds inside a nominal recasting.** A construct relation can license the English preposition used for it, but not a supplied lexical participle: `חֲמַס אֶרֶץ` → *violence done to the land* gives *violence* to the construct noun and *to the land* to its dependent under rule 19, while *done* is `added` because no source verb licenses it. This is not rule 31's generic completion of a substantive's lexeme: *done* predicates an event of the violence rather than naming the violence. **The copula goes to the predicate, and where a predicate morpheme is present an explicit subject takes only its own English.** Where the clause writes its subject — a pronoun such as `אָנֹכִי`, `אֲנִי`, `אַתְּ` or `הוּא`, or a subject noun — that morpheme takes the English pronoun or noun realizing it and nothing more, while the supplied *am*, *art*, *is*, *are* or *was* joins the predicate, exactly as rule 49 puts it on the preposition heading a prepositional predicate and rule 34 puts it on the predicate a gapped line licenses. `עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם אָנֹכִי` → *I* ***am*** *Abraham's servant* gives *am* to `עֶבֶד` and *I* to `אָנֹכִי`; `בַּת מִי אַתְּ` → *Whose daughter* ***art*** *thou* gives *art* to `בַּת`; `הוּא אֲדֹנִי` → *It* ***is*** *my master* gives *is* to `אֲדֹנִי`; and `מִי הָאִישׁ הַלָּזֶה` → *What man* ***is*** *this* gives *is* to `מִי`, which is the clause's predicate, leaving *this* to the demonstrative. **Where the predicate is wholly elided and no predicate morpheme is available to bear the construction-supplied copula, the copula instead joins the explicit subject as the clause's sole overt anchor:** `אֲנִי` → *I am*. This exception does not apply where a predicate is written. **And a copula the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary belongs to the interrogative particle, not to the predicate.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in a verbless clause and the ASV writes a single *Is*, *Am*, *Art*, *Are* or *Was* at the clause head, that one word is both this rule's construction-supplied copula and the question auxiliary rule 17 gives the particle: the particle takes it and heads on it, and the predicate keeps only its own English. `הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ` → ***Is*** *not thy fear of God thy confidence* gives *Is* to `הֲ` and leaves `כִּסְלָה` the bare *confidence*. This is rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause holding for a verbless clause with any predicate, and rule 17's *belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb* holding where there is no verb to compete for the word. Where the ASV writes a second copula for the predicate itself, that one is the predicate's under this rule's earlier sentences; where no interrogative morpheme stands in the clause, there is no particle to take it and those sentences govern alone. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, since the copula stands beside the subject in every one of these; where the predicate's own words then stand apart from it, the unit is discontinuous under rule 25.
**Rule 20 also governs an identifying formula where the ASV repeats one subject pronoun as both an English subject demonstrative and a predicate determiner.** Both realizations belong to that pronoun in one discontinuous unit, while the copula still goes to the written predicate: `הוּא אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה` → *These are that Aaron and Moses* gives *These ... that* to `הוּא`, headed on *These*, and *are Aaron* to `אַהֲרֹן`. The repeated demonstrative is not `added`; it is the ASV's emphatic identifying expansion of the single pronoun.
amendments.why: Rule 20's 'the copula goes to the predicate' was unqualified for interrogative clauses, while rule 17 gives a fronted question auxiliary to the particle and rule 50 states the same for interrogative existentials. JOB.4.6 is the case neither reaches: a verbless clause with a nominal predicate whose single 'Is' is at once the copula and the question auxiliary, which the chapter gave to הֲ. The corpus agrees and does not contradict — הֲ is aligned to 'is' in 25 units, to 'art' in 5, to 'am' in the verbless JOB.7.12, to 'are they' at MIC.1.5 and to 'is it' at EZK.20.3 and HAB.2.13 — and rule 50's existential sentence is the same ruling in a narrower place, so the qualification belongs in rule 20's own text rather than as a new rule pointing back at it.

amendments.rule: Where one Hebrew substantive is rendered by a multi-word English phrase, head it on the word carrying the lexeme rather than on the word the ASV supplies to complete the phrase. Decide which is which by dropping each word in turn: the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `יַבָּשָׁה` → *dry land* heads on *dry*, because *land* alone is any land; `בָּמָה` → *high place*, *high places* heads on *high*, because *place* alone is any place; so too `קֹדֶשׁ` → *holy place*, `מִסְתָּר` → *secret places*, `תִּמֹרָה` → *palm trees*, `עֹלָה` → *burnt offerings*. **Neither part of speech nor position decides this.** The supplied word is usually the English phrase's head noun and the lexeme-bearing word usually an attributive adjective standing first, but do not move a head onto a generic noun merely because it is the noun — that reasoning would head *dry land* on *land* — and do not reach for the first word as a rule. Where the ASV supplies the modifier instead, the same test moves the head the other way: `תַּנִּין` → *sea monsters* heads on *monsters*, because *sea* is a specifier added to a word that already names the creature. **Where the subtraction test ties, read the ASV's own use of the English noun.** A class noun the ASV writes alone for a Hebrew word of that same class — in the verse, in the passage, or as its ordinary rendering of the word before you — is not a supplied generic but the word that realizes the lexeme, and a modifier standing beside it is the ASV's specifier distinguishing one class word from another, so the head stays on the class noun: JOB.4.10-11 writes a bare *lion* for `אַרְיֵה` and *the fierce lion*, *the young lions* and *The old lion* for `שַׁחַל`, `כְּפִיר` and `לַיִשׁ`, and all four head on *lion*; JOB.4.17 writes *a man* for `גֶּבֶר` and *mortal man* for `אֱנוֹשׁ`, and both head on *man*; `יֶתֶר` → *tent cord* heads on *cord*. Where the ASV never writes that noun alone for the word — *place* for `בָּמָה`, *sleep* for `תַּרְדֵּמָה` → *deep sleep* — the noun is the supplied generic and the head is the modifier, as above. Ask which of the two the English noun is before choosing, and say in the note that the other reading was available. Where the phrase also carries an article, *of*, or *a*, rules 19 and 29 place those; they are never the head. **A substantival numeral is such a substantive.** Where the ASV completes a numeral standing for what it counts with a generic noun the Hebrew does not write, that noun joins the numeral’s unit and the head stays on the numeral, which carries the lexeme: `אֶחָד` → *one* ***portion*** in a list of tribal allotments, `אֶחָד` → *the* ***first day***. Rule 33’s `added` case is the other one, and what the supplied noun does tells them apart: there the numeral is a quantity whose English is already complete and the noun names the unit it is counted in — the italic ***reeds*** after *five and twenty thousand* — so the numeral’s own rendering loses nothing when it is dropped.
amendments.why: Rule 31 gave the תַּנִּין ruling as a conclusion ('sea is a specifier added to a word that already names the creature') without a test for recognizing that case, and its subtraction test ties whenever both words could be read as the lexeme-bearer. JOB.4 had to decide the family four times in two verses and decided it inconsistently, which is the split this pass patched: four lion-words and two man-words, where the ASV's own bare renderings of אַרְיֵה and גֶּבֶר show which word carries the class. The addition is a diagnostic for the tie the rule already acknowledges, it leaves every one of rule 31's stated examples standing (place, land, tree, offering are all nouns the ASV never writes alone for those words), and no corpus row shown contradicts it.

conventions: Where the ASV renders one Hebrew noun by a specifier plus an English class noun, and writes that same class noun alone for another Hebrew word of the same class in the context, the head goes on the class noun and the specifier is read as the ASV's disambiguation: JOB.4.10-11's שַׁחַל, כְּפִיר and לַיִשׁ head on 'lion(s)' beside the bare 'lion' of אַרְיֵה, JOB.4.17's אֱנוֹשׁ heads on 'man' beside the bare 'a man' of גֶּבֶר, and JOB.4.21's יֶתֶר heads on 'cord'. The specifier keeps the head only where the English noun is a generic the ASV never writes alone for that word — תַּרְדֵּמָה to 'deep sleep' at JOB.4.13, which is rule 31's 'high place' family.

מִן + בְּלִי is fused into one unit at JOB.4.20 ('without') and split at JOB.4.11 ('for lack'), and כְּ + אֲשֶׁר is split at JOB.4.8 ('According as'). Each follows rule 30's one-rendering condition read off the ASV, so the same morpheme pair analysed two ways in one chapter is not a split where the ASV writes a single English word in one place and a word per morpheme in the other.

JOB.4.18: where the ASV swaps roles — promoting the object of a written preposition to its verb's direct object and reaching the Hebrew's bare accusative through a preposition it supplies — the written preposition is unrepresented under rule 40 and the supplied one joins the verb's unit under rule 44. 'his angels he chargeth with folly' leaves בְ on מַלְאָכָיו with nothing to say and gives 'with' to יָשִׂים, whose object תָּהֳלָה carries no marker and no preposition of its own. BSB, which attaches a preposition to its own phrase, disagrees here by convention, not by a defect in the alignment.

report: Read all 21 verses end to end and every one of the 19 candidate groups. Eighteen groups are the ASV rendering one word differently in different contexts, licensed by the source: אֶל to 'with'/'unto' (4.2, 4.5); מִן comparative 'more than' (4.17) against the range-opening 'Betwixt' (4.20); waw to 'Then', 'and', 'Now', 'but', 'Or', 'and that', each read off the ASV under rule 14; הַ to 'the' where a 'the' is written (4.19) against unrepresented where none is (4.20, rule 12); הֲ to 'If'/'Is'/'Shall' as the ASV's clause frame differs.

One real split, invisible to the lemma table because it is a head placement and not an edge. A single Hebrew noun rendered by an ASV specifier plus an English class noun heads on the class noun four times — שַׁחַל to 'the fierce lion' and כְּפִיר to 'the young lions' (4.10), לַיִשׁ to 'The old lion' (4.11), all beside the bare 'lion' the same passage writes for אַרְיֵה, and יֶתֶר to 'tent cord' (4.21) — but on the specifier at 4.17, אֱנוֹשׁ to 'mortal man', in the very verse where גֶּבֶר to 'a man' heads on 'man'. Patched 4.17: s002's target head moves from t002 'mortal' to t003 'man'. Unit membership is unchanged and the competing reading is named in the unit's note.

Left 4.13's תַּרְדֵּמָה to 'deep sleep' headed on 'deep'. It is not the same construction: 'sleep' is a generic the ASV never writes alone for that word, which puts it in rule 31's 'high place' family rather than its 'sea monsters' one. The boundary is recorded as a convention and promoted as an amendment to rule 31.

BSB disagreements: neither is an error. JOB.4.4 ן is a paragogic nun, its own unrepresented unit under rule 32, which BSB attaches to its host — the documented convention difference. JOB.4.18 בְ on מַלְאָכָיו is a genuine analysis difference rather than a mistake: the ASV writes 'his angels' bare and spends its 'with' before the bare accusative תָּהֳלָה, so by the subtraction test of rules 16 and 44 that word answers to the English verb's valency and not to the preposition's own relation, leaving בְ unrepresented under rule 40. BSB attaches a preposition to its own phrase. The verse already records the competing reading; no accepted edge was changed to improve the comparison rate.

Checked the added units and the supplied English the lemma table cannot see. All three added units (4.6 'of God', 4.16 'saying', 4.20 'it') are English no morpheme licenses, and every supplied 'the', 'a', subject pronoun, copula, relative and antecedent elsewhere in the chapter goes to the morpheme that licenses it — consistently across 4.3, 4.4, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9, 4.10, 4.11, 4.13, 4.16, 4.19, 4.20. Phrasal particles ('cut off', 'scattered abroad', 'stood up', 'plucked up') keep the head on the verb in all five places, and light verbs ('made firm', 'made to shake', 'putteth trust') head on the complement in all three. No second patch.

מִן+בְּלִי is fused at 4.20 ('without') and split at 4.11 ('for lack'), and כְּ+אֲשֶׁר is split at 4.8 ('According as'). These are rule 30's one-rendering condition read off the ASV, not a split; recorded as a convention because they are the chapter's most split-looking pair.

Two amendments returned: rule 20, for the copula of a verbless clause that the ASV fronts as a question auxiliary (4.6), which rule 50 already settles for existentials and rule 17 for verbal clauses; and rule 31, for the tie its own subtraction test leaves in the specifier-plus-class-noun family, which is what this chapter had to decide four times.
